text.bold: 1. The source of protein doesn't change the result.

paragraph.text: In 2021, Hevia-Larraín and colleagues followed young vegans and omnivores through 12 weeks of resistance training, with protein intake matched at 1.6 g per kilogram per day. There was no difference in muscle mass, fiber area or strength. To reach that amount, the vegans used soy protein powder.

text.bold: 2. With enough protein, the difference is small or nil.

paragraph.text: A 2018 meta-analysis found no difference between supplementing soy protein or animal protein in gains in mass and strength from resistance training. Another, from 2021, also found no difference in strength or absolute lean mass, but found a small advantage for animal protein in the lean mass of younger adults. The difference appears in some studies, is small, and can be offset with more plant protein.
In many sports, vegan athletes compete and win at a high level. This shows the diet doesn't prevent performance.
The US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics considers well-planned vegan diets adequate for athletes too.

text.bold: 5. "Nobody builds muscle without meat" is false.

Athletes have greater needs, and it's true that reaching high protein intakes takes more planning on a vegan diet. It's also true that studies on the subject are still relatively small.
But the available evidence and high-level vegan athletes show that meat isn't necessary. The protein muscles need can come from plants.
